tweets.text:
This article from @ArrakisFinance is one of the most extensive analyses I've seen of tokenised equity holder profiles and behaviour.

FYI, it looks at things like:

→ Custody distribution
→ Holder concentration
→ Position size
→ Holding periods
→ Trading activity
→ Differences across issuers and chains

The most striking thing is how different the holder base looks depending on the issuer.

@Ondo has around 80% of its end-user value in self-custody, while @bstocksfinance has just 8%.

Even within @Ondo, the split changes a lot by chain. Self-custody is ~97% on Ethereum and roughly half on BNB Chain.

You can’t really treat tokenised equity holders as one group when the holder mix changes this much depending on the issuer and chain.

Solid piece.
Happy to contribute to this shared knowledge.

tweets.text:
China added more solar last year than the entire worlds standing stock of solar. 

This is Wright's Law doing what it always does... every time cumulative production doubles, the cost falls by a fixed percentage. Solar has sat on that curve for decades. China just poured scale into it.

So the cost of creating energy is collapsing. Meanwhile compute costs are collapsing too. The per token cost of intelligence is on its own Wright's Law curve.

The input, energy, and the output, intelligence, are both falling in cost at once... a double exponential. Cheaper energy makes cheaper compute. Cheaper compute makes more intelligence, which makes energy cheaper again. That flywheel is The Exponential Age... technologies feeding each other rather than advancing alone.

It is scary how fast it is already. We aint seen nothing yet.

Daniel Ek: The US is spending 18% of its GDP on healthcare. It's the single largest line item in the budget right now. Preventable chronic disease is the biggest drive.

“The US is spending 18% of its GDP on healthcare. It's the single largest line item in the budget right now.

And if you take heart disease alone, it's in the hundreds of billions of dollars that are being spent on that disease group in the US alone. It's just insane. It's larger than Fortune 10 companies' revenues.

And so I started looking into everything from drugs, to can you make more efficient drugs? Is it about cancers? And basically started targeting like, what are the real reasons it looks that way?

The real conclusion ended up being there's lots of reasons, not one.

But the major one is really chronic disease, overall. And the crazy thing about chronic disease, when you read about it, is that if you discover these things early, they're totally preventable, and the cost of dealing with them is very small, and the suffering for the person and their family and community is very small, too.

So the key thing is if you discover things early, you're actually good.

And so then the question is, well, why don't we discover things early?

And it happens to be that we don't have enough data. So everyone in the entire healthcare industry is in agreement that we have to take healthcare from reactive to preventative health.

Our view is really that it all starts with having better data. If you have better data, you're going to be able to discover things much more easily, and that in itself will then lead to having a chance of discovering those things much earlier, which creates this virtuous flywheel of then changing healthcare.”
